doc.title: Chuck Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 7, 2023

title: Opening piano improvisation at Hamilton College
summary: Lamb plays an introduction on the grand piano and says each piano has a voice from which themes emerge; Rowe says improvising is magic.

story.theme_name: Opening the interview: Monk Rowe's welcome and archive boilerplate
story.community_name: Opening the Hamilton College interview: introductions and boilerplate

blocks.x: I’m very pleased to have Chuck Lamb today at the — returning to the scene of a concert, you know it was almost a year ago when you played here with the Brubeck Brothers at Hamilton College.
That was an awesome concert. So before the quote tape was rolling, you were playing a little introduction so could I request an interview introduction?

Sure. And you know I was just telling you that when I do these tours with the Brubecks and get into the hall and it’s usually pretty quiet and they have these beautiful grand pianos and I turn on my recorder because every piano has some sort of voice and this has a ton of music in it so I’ll just see what pops out right now.

Oh yeah. I’m going to dub in some applause because it’s worth it. You know I know classical people who would really envy that ability and I’m going to stay here for a moment and first of all you said there’s a lot of music in this piano. What does that actually mean for you?

The sound of the instrument, you know like when I got here like I explained before with the Brubeck thing, I did that with this piano and four or five different themes came out immediately. You know? Just letting my hands fall and start to improvise off of the reaction I get from the instrument. And you know that’s developed over a long period of time to have the trust to be able to do that, just to sit down and let my hands fall.

So these themes, just, they come out and they start singing to me and I just let my hands follow it, you know. It’s pretty, you know, obviously superfast how that happens and you react instantly to it but it’s one of my biggest joys is to let that stuff emerge as it will. It’s really —
I’ve always thought it’s improvising, especially this type of thing that you’re doing, can only be explained so far. There’s a magic to it that, at least I can’t put it into words and
